lines.text: Speculative decoding is the trick for making a model write faster without changing it.
A small draft model proposes a batch of tokens. The big model checks them all in one pass.
If the draft was right, you take the tokens. If it was wrong, you take the first one and start again.
So the speedup is not the size of the draft model. It is how often the draft is right.
At full acceptance you get the maximum speedup, which is the batch size you used.
At zero acceptance you get nothing, and you have paid for the draft model on every token.
Most real systems sit somewhere in between. Roughly sixty to eighty percent is typical.
Which is why a draft model that is barely better than the big one can still be useless.
It has to be close enough to guess right, and small enough to be cheap.
There is a second cost people forget. Every rejected token is wasted work for both models.
So a low acceptance rate does not just slow you down. It makes you do more work than the baseline.
The speedup is not the draft model. It is the agreement.
